definition: Repression: the mechanism by which representations linked to a drive are kept in the unconscious. Freud distinguishes primal repression (Urverdrängung, which creates the unconscious) from secondary repression (eigentliche Verdrängung, which pushes derivatives back). For Lacan, repression operates on signifiers: the repressed signifier remains within the symbolic order as unconscious, producing return-of-the-repressed symptoms.

contrasts.differential: Repression keeps the signifier in the symbolic unconscious (neurosis); foreclosure (forclusion/Verwerfung) expels the signifier from the symbolic altogether (psychosis)
Repression bars the signifier from consciousness; Verneinung (negation) allows its content to appear in consciousness in negated form ('It is NOT my mother')

definition: Drive: a constant force (konstante Kraft) that has a source, pressure, aim, and object, but unlike instinct has no natural object. The drive circles around the object (objet a) without ever reaching it — its satisfaction lies in the circuit itself, not in the attainment of the object. Lacan identifies four partial drives: oral, anal, scopic, and invocatory.

contrasts.differential: The drive circles around its object in a constant loop; desire is sustained by the metonymy of lack and the gap between demand and need
Instinct has a natural biological object and aim; the drive has no predetermined object and its aim is the circuit itself
The drive is the structural mechanism; jouissance is the excessive satisfaction it produces beyond the pleasure principle

definition: Desire: the metonymy of lack, constituted in the gap between demand and need. Desire is always the desire of the Other — it is directed beyond any particular object and can never be satisfied. Unlike need (which is biological and satisfiable) and demand (which is need articulated in language plus an unconditional demand for love), desire is the unsatisfiable remainder.

contrasts.differential: Need is biological and can be satisfied; desire is symbolic and constitutively unsatisfiable
Demand is need articulated in language; desire is what remains after need is subtracted from demand
Desire sustains itself through lack; jouissance is the excessive satisfaction beyond the pleasure principle that aims to abolish lack

definition: Subject: the divided subject ($, S barré) constituted by the signifier, barred from full self-knowledge by the unconscious. The subject is not the ego (moi) but the effect of the signifying chain — 'a signifier represents the subject for another signifier.' The subject is what appears in the intervals of the signifying chain and vanishes when pinned down.

contrasts.differential: The subject is the divided effect of the signifier; the ego (moi) is an imaginary construction based on mirror-identifications
The subject is constituted by the Other; the Other is the locus of the signifier from which the subject receives its own message in inverted form

definition: Enjoyment beyond the pleasure principle: an excessive, painful satisfaction that transgresses homeostatic limits. Jouissance is what the pleasure principle works to avoid — it is not pleasure (Lust) but an excessive excitation that the organism cannot regulate. Lacan distinguishes phallic jouissance (subject to castration and the signifier), jouissance of the Other (beyond the phallic), and the jouissance of meaning (joui-sens).

contrasts.differential: Pleasure (plaisir) operates within homeostatic limits; jouissance transgresses those limits toward an unbearable excess
Desire is sustained by lack; jouissance aims at its abolition in fullness
The drive is the structural mechanism; jouissance is the satisfaction produced in the drive's circuit around the object

definition: Signifier: the material element of the symbolic order that represents the subject for another signifier. For Lacan (departing from Saussure), the signifier has primacy over the signified — meaning is an effect of the signifying chain, not a pre-existing content that the signifier merely expresses. The signifier is pure differential value with no positive content.

contrasts.differential: The signifier is the material form with primacy; the signified is the meaning effect that slides beneath the signifying chain
For Saussure the sign unites signifier and signified; for Lacan the bar between them is resistant, and the signifier dominates

definition: Signified: the meaning effect produced by the play of signifiers in the symbolic chain. Unlike Saussure's stable signified, Lacan's signified is always sliding beneath the signifier — it is not a fixed content but a retroactive effect of the signifying chain's operation. Only at the point de capiton is the sliding temporarily arrested.

contrasts.differential: The signified is meaning; the signifier is material form. The signifier has logical priority
Sens (sense/meaning) is the effect of signifier articulation; the signified is the particular meaning attributed to a signifier, always unstable

definition: The Imaginary: one of Lacan's three registers (with the Symbolic and Real). The order of images, identifications, and the dual relation, founded on the mirror stage. The Imaginary provides illusory wholeness, the gestalt of the body image, and narcissistic identification. It is the domain of the ego (moi) and méconnaissance (misrecognition).

contrasts.differential: The Imaginary operates through resemblance and wholeness; the Symbolic through difference and lack
The Imaginary provides illusory completeness; the Real exposes its impossibility

definition: The Symbolic: one of Lacan's three registers. The order of language, law, social structure, and the unconscious that constitutes the subject through signification. The Symbolic is structured by the signifier and governed by the Name-of-the-Father. It is the domain of the Other (Autre), of prohibition, and of the constitution of desire.

contrasts.differential: The Symbolic operates through differential signifiers; the Imaginary through images and resemblance
The Symbolic structures reality through language; the Real is what absolutely resists symbolization

definition: The Real: that which resists symbolization absolutely, the impossible kernel that can be neither imagined nor spoken. The Real is not 'reality' (which is structured by the Symbolic and Imaginary) but what remains as an irreducible remainder after all symbolization. It is encountered as trauma, anxiety, and the impasses of formalization.

contrasts.differential: The Real is what cannot be symbolized; the Symbolic is the order of language and law
The Real shatters imaginary wholeness; the Imaginary is the domain of images and identification
Reality is the social construction of Symbolic and Imaginary; the Real is what disrupts this construction
